items.abstract: <jats:p>The control code is an essential part of achieving energy-saving control in HVAC systems. Although there are existing methods for automatically generating control code, these methods still largely rely on expert knowledge for intervention. HVAC systems are highly personalized, with varying types of equipment, different quantities of equipment, and diverse data transmission protocols, all of which still require manual processing, resulting in low efficiency and a strong dependence on human input. To address this challenge, a method based on large language models is proposed. The basic idea is to leverage the understanding, reasoning, and coding capabilities of large language models, provide sufficient information to the model using the RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) technique, and validate the accuracy of the code through a simulation model. By iterating repeatedly, the accuracy of the code is improved, ultimately enabling the automatic generation of control code. The evaluation used 173 laboratory rooms from an actual project to verify the efficiency and accuracy of this method. The results show that this method is highly efficient, processing a single room in just 5 min, and performs well under project-specific conditions, with a code generation accuracy of 97.1%.</jats:p>
title: Large Language Model-Based Method for HVAC System Control Code Automatic Generation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Students  find it difficult to learn the syntax of programming languages when they are  new to coding. Some students get discouraged and even quit their coding journey  because of having trouble with memorizing all the syntactic rules of a  programming language. Flowcharts are an effective way to help students  visualize the logic of an algorithm developed to solve a problem. But some  students find it challenging to convert their flowcharts into executable code  and even when they do, some get frustrated because of the errors they encounter  while running the code they have written. So students who are not well versed  with the syntax of a programming language can face difficulty debugging their  programs even when they understand the logic behind the algorithms. This  research aimed at developing a tool that can assist young students with less  coding experience to learn programming. An intuitive user interface for the  application was developed using a python library called gradio. The  functionality of taking flowchart images as user inputs and providing  equivalent python code with a brief explanation was incorporated on the UI.  Text from the uploaded flowchart image is extracted in 3 steps which include  feature extraction using deep learning models like ResNet and VGG, sequence  labelling using Long Short-Term Memory networks and decoding the sequence  labels using Connectionist Temporal Classification algorithms. The extracted  text is then provided to an open source large language model with 70 billion  parameters called Llama-2-Chat for the generation of the python code. The  generated python code is displayed on the gradio UI along with a brief  explanation of the code. The user can copy the code and run it on the IDE of  their choice. The application was evaluated with a test dataset of several  flowchart images. The generated python codes for the test flowchart images were  executed in a code editor and the produced outputs were found to be correct.  The generated code got executed without any errors for 75 % of the flowchart  images from the test dataset.</jats:p>
title: Code Generation from Flowchart using Optical Character Recognition & Large Language Model

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced the field of Automated Software Engineering (ASE), particularly in code generation tasks. Their performance continues to improve with scale, both in terms of model size and training data. While LLMs have demonstrated strong capabilities on existing datasets, many of these benchmarks are either language-specific, overly simplified, or limited to function-level code, offering limited insight into real-world software development scenarios. Recent benchmarks, like ClassEval, attempt to address this gap, but a lack of broader datasets that reflect realistic system-level requirements persists, especially in the context of evaluating LLMs for end-to-end code generation. In response, a novel dataset designed to simulate real-world subsystems of large-scale information systems was presented. Starting from detailed functional requirements, the dataset includes object-oriented models, physical data models, and program logic specifications, represented as Class Diagrams, Data Definition Language scripts, and Structured English, respectively. The dataset was carefully designed within the practical constraints of LLMs, including token limits and computational overhead. Preliminary evaluations show that LLMs can effectively interpret the models and generate functional code, demonstrating the dataset's potential as a benchmark for realistic, system-level code generation. This work is anticipated to serve as a foundation for further research into scalable, real-world datasets for LLM-driven software engineering.</jats:p>
title: A System-level Software Requirements Dataset for Large Language Model Code Generation

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>Large Language Models have received a lot of attention in recent years due to their outstanding performance on various Natural Language Processing tasks. They can be used for lots of applications, including assistance in code generation tasks. Actual literature lacks an exhaustive analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of using a Large Language Model for the generation of simple and complex code. This paper aims to overcome the issue: we perform a Literature Review to explore the state-of-the-art of the proposed topic, answering 4 Research Questions. Using the PRISMA methodology, we reviewed 66 papers published between 2021 and 2023. Our analysis reveals Python’s dominance as the preferred language and identifies a significant research gap in addressing ethical constraints. Additionally, we provide insights into the performance of models such as GPT-4 and CodeLlama, and their comparative utility in tasks ranging from debugging to multi-turn program synthesis. The findings offer a foundation for future research aimed at optimizing LLMs for code generation.</jats:p>
title: Usage of Large Language Model for Code Generation Tasks: A Review

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has created new opportunities to automate software development activities, including generating source code from software requirements. However, achieving consistent, accurate, and traceable code generation remains challenging due to the ambiguity of requirements models and the variability of prompt formulations used to interact with LLMs. While prompt engineering has emerged as a critical factor influencing LLM performance, existing prompt pattern catalogues primarily address general-purpose interactions and provide limited support for requirements-model-driven code generation. This paper presents a specialized catalogue of prompt patterns designed to guide the transformation of software requirements models into executable code artefacts. The proposed catalogue identifies and organizes reusable prompt patterns that support key activities in the code generation process, including requirements interpretation, clarification, validation, context preservation, iterative refinement, and code synthesis. A preliminary evaluation using ChatGPT-5 and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct demonstrated that the proposed prompt patterns effectively guided model-to-code generation from software requirements models while improving contextual consistency and implementation fidelity. The catalogue aims to improve the quality, consistency, and reliability of AI-assisted model-to-code transformations by providing a structured framework for constructing prompts. Furthermore, the study positions prompt patterns as a bridge between requirements engineering and generative AI, contributing a domain-specific perspective to the growing body of research on prompt engineering. The catalogue serves as a foundation for future empirical investigations and tool-supported approaches for integrating LLMs into model-driven software engineering workflows.</jats:p>
title: A Prompt Pattern Catalogue for Requirements-Model-driven Code Generation using Large Language Models
